(a) offline RL can be used to improve reproducibility and simplify deep RL research, (b) REM is a simple and effective algorithm for off-policy deep RL.
(1) offline RL can help simplify deep RL algorithms, and (2) a simple Q-learning method can achieve state-of-the-art results on Atari 260.

In summary, our research is concerned with

the following questions: (1) How can we isolate the effects of exploitation vs exploration in off-policy RL algorithms? (2) How can we design simpler deep RL algorithms? (3) How can we improve the reproducibility of RL research?
the design of simpler, more robust deep RL algorithms, and the development of an offline RL benchmark for the evaluation of such algorithms.
the design of simpler algorithms for deep RL, and we hope that our results will encourage future research in this direction.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the use of offline RL can help us better understand the contributions of exploitation and exploration in off-policy RL and facilitate the development of simpler RL algorithms.
the use of offline RL can improve the reproducibility, robustness and simplicity of deep RL research.
REM outperforms DQN, C51, and QR-DQN, and is comparable to Rainbow on the offline Atari 2600 benchmark.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the performance of off-policy deep RL agents is not limited by the exploration/exploitation trade-off.
we advocate the use of offline reinforcement learning (RL), and propose Random Ensemble Mixture, a simple off-policy RL algorithm that outperforms complex baselines in an offline setting.
we have proposed a new benchmark for offline RL and have demonstrated that simpler algorithms can be competitive with state-of-the-art algorithms.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the design of simple algorithms that exploit offline data can be as fruitful as the design of more complex algorithms that exploit online data.
simple Q-learning algorithms, such as REM, can outperform complex off-policy deep RL methods when trained on logged data.
the exploration-exploitation tradeoff is not a fundamental barrier to achieving state-of-the-art RL performance in practice.
